source.title: Pulling The REINS: Training-Free Safety Alignment of Video Diffusion Models via Representation Steering
source.authors: Rohit Kundu; Arindam Dutta; Sarosij Bose; Athula Balachandran; A. Roy-Chowdhury

page_placements.theme: Safety and concept steering in video diffusion and physics models (analogues outside language models)

record.file_problem: None; full paper and appendices are present. Some table content is flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests a related single-direction safety-steering idea in video diffusion models, a different modality and behavior from refusal in safety-trained chat models. Its results are an extension, not a direct test of the stated chat-model claims.
record.gate_note: The paper applies and evaluates an SPCA-discovered safety direction in video diffusion models, reporting safety outcomes, quality metrics, a rank ablation, and layer-dependent steering results. These are relevant to the single-direction safety-steering analogy, but the models generate videos rather than answer users, and the measured behavior is safe-versus-unsafe video generation rather than refusal. The paper cites the original LLM refusal result as an analogy; that citation is not treated as evidence. Hyperparameter-selection values and results for other methods are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study covers video diffusion models, which produce safe or unsafe videos. It has no chat model, no refusal of a user, and no harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction. It adds, rather than ablates, an SPCA direction learned from safety-classifier labels. It cites Arditi et al. only as motivation, calling its rank-1 result a 'video-domain analogue' of that finding. Its results are about a related but different construct (steering video safety), so no version is tested. The reader's 'tests'/T3 is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that safety is linearly encoded in video diffusion hidden states and that a single SPCA direction, added at an intermediate layer, raises safety across 9 models. They say this preserves quality and is robust to adversarial prompts where prompt filtering fails. They call the rank-1 result a video-domain analogue of the LLM refusal-direction finding. This is an analogy, not a test of it.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SPCA on binary safety-classifier labels from video generations, then adds a direction to an intermediate video-transformer layer during early denoising, with per-channel norm preservation. It does not use the stated harmful-minus-harmless instruction difference, remove a direction, or test chat refusal.
record.method_sensitivity: Effect depends on intervention layer: early layers are ineffective, intermediate layers work best, and late layers can cause generation collapse. The optimal steering strength varies across models. The main evaluation also reports results across two safety benchmarks and an adversarial video-prompt set.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding an SPCA safety direction at an intermediate layer raises classifier-rated safety rates in all 9 video diffusion models on SafeSora and SafeWatch-Bench (mean +0.22 / +0.21).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In video diffusion transformers, a single label-supervised hidden-state direction can steer generations toward classifier-safe outputs.

fits_no_version.finding: Steered-versus-baseline VideoAlign win rates vary widely, from 25.5% to 80.0%. Several fall below parity, e.g. Allegro SafeSora VQ at 25.5%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Video safety steering has model- and benchmark-dependent quality costs.

fits_no_version.finding: A direction calibrated on SafeSora raises the Wan2.1 safety rate on MMA-Diffusion adversarial prompts from 0.42 to 0.79.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hidden-state safety steering in video models holds up against prompt-level adversarial attacks.

fits_no_version.finding: A rank-1 direction captures about 68% of safety-relevant variance and reaches about 0.98 safety rate at high λ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Video-generation safety is low-dimensional in hidden-state space.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering is ineffective at early layers, works at about 50% depth, and collapses generation at late layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In video diffusion safety steering, the intervention layer trades information availability against downstream propagation.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering moves unsafe generations across the safe/unsafe boundary in the SPCA projection, under both in-domain and OOD classifiers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The steering shift is representational and not specific to the calibration classifier.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says the codebase will be released upon acceptance.
record.problems: The reported safety rates rely on trained safety classifiers. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for its main quantitative results. Late-layer steering can produce generation collapse, so a high safety rate there does not establish useful safe generation. The table's I2V section is flattened in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: I2V VQ and MQ values were not extracted because the flattened Table 2 text does not support confident assignment of those quality values to individual models and benchmarks. Individual numerical points from Fig. 3 were not extracted; the text-described early, intermediate, and late-layer outcomes are recorded in r47-r49. The table's mean-across-models quality values and lambda calibration sweep were omitted because they are aggregates or hyperparameter-selection results rather than separate model-condition outcomes.

untested.parts: All: no chat model, no refusal, no difference-in-means direction, no ablation, no induced refusal.
All: no weight edit, no released chat models.
All: MMA-Diffusion is a prompt attack on video models and is not analysed as suppressing a refusal direction; no adversarial training.
All: the rank ablation concerns video-safety steering subspaces, not chat refusal.
All: transfer is across video architectures and T2V/I2V, not LLM languages, variants or base/instruct.

record.verdict_notes: The study is a different modality and a different behaviour (unsafe content generation, not refusal). It adds a supervised direction rather than ablating a difference-in-means direction. It is not an original source. No verdicts are given. Safety rates come from the authors' own trained SigLIP classifier, and no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: No safety-trained chat model, refusal behavior, difference-in-means harmful-minus-harmless direction, direction ablation, or induced refusal to harmless user requests is tested.
No weight edit or released-model chat refusal evaluation is tested.
The paper evaluates an external video-prompt attack, not attacks that suppress a chat-model refusal direction or training against such an ablation.
The rank ablation concerns video-generation safety, not whether chat-model refusal is affine, conical, or distributed across refusal directions.
No harmfulness judgment is separated from a chat model's refusal decision.
The paper tests video-model architectures and T2V/I2V settings, not transfer of an LLM refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
No comparison of chat-model refusal training methods or timing is conducted.

rows.operation_detail: A rank-1 SPCA safety direction is used for steering and compared with higher-rank steering subspaces.
rows.measure: Safety rate and safety-relevant variance captured
rows.value: Rank-1 captures approximately 68% of safety-relevant variance and reaches ∼0.98 safety rate with sufficient λ; higher ranks do not significantly improve safety rate, VQ, or MQ.
rows.note: A rank-1 video safety-steering result, not a test of refusal directions in chat models.
rows.check: The value says higher ranks do not significantly improve metrics; that matches the Fig. 5 caption. The Sec. 3.2 text instead says higher ranks 'marginally improve safety but at a steeper VQ/MQ cost'. The note should carry both. The subject should be marked as not specified in the text.

source_check.problem: none; ~68% and ~0.98 are in the text; caption says higher ranks don't help significantly, Sec. 3.2 says 'marginally improve safety' at a steeper VQ/MQ cost; the model used is not stated

relation.reason: Arditi et al. [29] appears twice, as an analogy: the rank-1 choice 'mirrors prior findings' (Sec. 2.3), and its result is a 'video-domain analogue of the one-dimensional refusal finding' (Sec. 3.2). There is no engagement beyond that; 'discusses' is at most arguable.

tranche.reason: Video diffusion models, safe/unsafe video generation scored by a video safety classifier; no chat model, no refusal of a user, no harmful-vs-harmless instruction contrast. It neither tests a version nor uses the refusal direction as a tool; Arditi et al. is cited only as an analogy for the rank-1 choice.

source_check.notes: Safety rates come from the authors' own SigLIP-based classifier, which also labelled the calibration set (OOD-classifier results are figure-only). 'Quality preserved' is overstated: mean VQ win rates are 38.9%/47.4%, and SafeSora VQ is 12-20% for the I2V models and 25.5% for Allegro. Per App. C.3/C.4 the 'single direction' is recomputed per timestep as a weighted sum of the top-6 SPCA components. My own derivation, not stated in the paper: with binary labels, Eq. A5 makes it a safe-minus-unsafe mean difference.

statements.problem: none; all 9 models improve on both benchmarks, the mean gains are +0.22 SafeSora / +0.21 SafeWatch-Bench (Table 2, Sec. 3.1), and rank-1 ~68% is in Sec. 3.2 / Fig. 5
